chapter_title: Security Best Practices for Web3.js dApps

screens.title: Security Best Practices for Web3.js dApps
screens.subtitle: Frontend protections for safe wallet interaction, validated inputs, and secret handling

narration.text: In this lesson we focus on the frontend side of dApp security. A smart contract can be well written, yet users still lose funds or trigger errors if the user interface fails to validate inputs, shows unclear transaction details, or exposes secret keys. You will learn how to detect and switch networks safely, validate addresses and amounts before sending transactions, protect users from phishing and misleading signing prompts, and keep A P I keys off the frontend by proxying through a secure backend. Each of these steps reduces real risk: network mismatches can cause failed or dangerous transactions, unchecked addresses can send funds to the wrong recipient, and exposed A P I keys can be abused. We will use concrete examples such as using the injected window. ethereum object, web3. utils. isAddress, and the wallet_switchEthereumChain request flow so you can implement checks and prompts in a React dApp. By the end, you will be able to add network checks, input validation, and secure A P I handling to your dApp, helping protect users and maintain trust.

keyIdea.title: Frontend security is essential
keyIdea.text: Protect users by validating inputs, enforcing correct network connection, preventing phishing, and keeping secrets off the client.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.4 › Security Best Practices
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Security Best Practices for Web3.js dApps

Frontend checks and patterns that keep users safe when connecting wallets, signing transactions, and sending data to smart contracts.

In this lesson

Network detection, input validation, and safe API key handling for Web3.js frontends.

Why it matters

A secure frontend prevents accidental fund loss and reduces attack surface beyond the smart contract itself.

Coming up

Concrete code snippets and a hands-on activity to add network checks and validation to your React dApp.

Explore Key Topics
Network Switching
Detect chainId and prompt safe switching to your target network.
Input Validation
Validate addresses and amounts with web3 utilities to avoid bad transactions.
Secrets & APIs
Never embed provider keys in the frontend; use a backend proxy instead.
Visual Concept
Wallet & Network
Detect chainId, show friendly prompts, and avoid dangerous cross-network transactions.
Input & Secrets
Validate addresses, amounts, and move API keys to a backend to reduce exposure.
Audit & Rate Limit
Keep dependencies updated and throttle backend endpoints to prevent abuse.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you will be able to do after this lesson

narration.text: By the end of this lesson you will recognize the primary frontend risks in Web3 dApps and implement practical defenses. First, you'll identify common attack vectors such as network mismatches, phishing prompts, and exposed A P I keys, and understand how they translate to user risk. Second, you'll be able to implement secure wallet connection patterns that detect the active chain, respond to chain and account changes, and guide users to switch networks safely. Third, you'll validate and sanitize user-provided addresses and numeric inputs so transactions are only sent with well-formed data. Finally, you'll learn how to keep secrets out of client code by proxying provider requests through a secure backend and how to apply rate limiting and dependency audits to reduce supply-chain and quota risks. Each objective includes a small mnemonic or check you can use while coding, and a milestone to verify competency so you can confirm your dApp behaves safely in real user flows.

keyIdea.title: Goals for this chapter
keyIdea.text: Detect networks, validate inputs, avoid exposing secrets, and implement defensive frontend patterns for user safety.

screens.title: How you'll demonstrate secure dApp skills
screens.subtitle: Four practical milestones to test your implementation

narration.text: This second objectives slide maps each milestone to a small verification step you can try in your dApp. For wallet connection, implement chain detection and deliberately connect MetaMask to the wrong network to confirm your prompt appears and your switch call works. For input validation, add a form that checks web3. utils. isAddress and numeric positivity and verify invalid values produce clear errors. For secret management, remove any provider keys from the frontend and replace them with a simple backend endpoint that forwards requests; test that your frontend no longer exposes keys in developer tools. Finally, for operational robustness, run a package audit and add simple rate limiting to any proxy endpoints so you observe how quota is preserved under burst requests. Each verification is intentional: you learn not only the code but the behavioral result a user will see. These checks make security practical and repeatable, and they serve as the base for further hardening and audits.

keyIdea.title: Practical verification steps
keyIdea.text: Small, repeatable tests prove each security control works and makes risks visible before deployment.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.4 › Verification Milestones

Verification checklist

Hands-on checks you can run immediately to confirm security behavior.

1. Chain mismatch test

Connect MetaMask to Mainnet while your dApp expects Sepolia and ensure the UI blocks risky actions and triggers wallet_switchEthereumChain.

2. Input validation test

Enter invalid addresses or negative amounts and verify clear errors prevent submission and conversion to Wei is correct for valid amounts.

3. Secret exposure check

Inspect network calls and source code to confirm provider keys are absent and backend proxy endpoints are used instead.

4. Rate limit and audit

Run package audit and simulate repeated backend calls to confirm rate limiting preserves service availability.

screens.title: Frontend security matters even with secure contracts
screens.subtitle: Why a secure UI is part of overall dApp safety

narration.text: A secure smart contract is necessary but not sufficient for user safety. The frontend mediates every user action: it shows addresses, builds transaction payloads, and requests signatures. If the UI omits a network check, a user connected to the wrong chain can either fail transactions or, in worst cases, send real funds to an unexpected contract. Similarly, a UI that formats numbers incorrectly or accepts invalid addresses can trigger incorrect transfers. A clear definition: frontend security is the set of practices that prevent user-facing errors, misleading prompts, and exposure of secrets when interacting with wallets and provider services. For example, a dApp that fails to show the to-address and the value before signing increases phishing risk; a well-constructed UI always surfaces that data and refuses to proceed on mismatch. A common misconception is that smart contract audits alone protect users; they do not address UI-level mistakes or stolen A P I keys. Takeaway: treat the frontend as a critical security layer. Quick check: can an attacker cause a user to sign a different transaction than shown? If yes, keep hardening.

keyIdea.title: Frontend is a security layer
keyIdea.text: UI mistakes can negate contract safety; always validate flows and show transaction details before signing.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.4 › Frontend Security
Definition

Frontend security

Practices that prevent user-facing errors, prevent misleading signing flows, and protect secrets used by the UI.

Concrete example
A dApp that refuses to proceed when MetaMask is on Mainnet but the contract is on Sepolia, preventing accidental real ETH transfers.
Common misconception
Audited contracts eliminate all risk. In reality, UI flaws and exposed keys create other attack vectors.
Key Takeaway

Treat the frontend as part of security: surface transaction details, validate data, and hide secrets.

Why this matters

Users rely on your UI to make safe choices. The frontend shapes the signing context and can either prevent or enable costly mistakes.

What to check
  • Network and account consistency
  • Explicit transaction details before signing
  • No secrets in client-side code
Try this
Connect with MetaMask, change chains, and observe whether your app blocks risky actions and prompts a network switch.

screens.title: Wallet connection and network detection
screens.subtitle: Detect chainId, handle events, and guide the user to the correct network

narration.text: Wallet connection is the first point where a dApp and a user meet, so it needs careful checks. The core claim is straightforward: always detect the connected chain and the active accounts, and subscribe to chainChanged and accountsChanged events so your UI reacts when the user switches networks or accounts. A concrete example is using the injected window. ethereum with Web3. js to get the chainId and to request accounts; if the chainId does not match your target chain, programmatically request a wallet switch with the wallet_switchEthereumChain method. A common mistake is assuming the user is on the correct network because they previously connected; chain and account state can change outside your app. Implement event handlers to reload or to gracefully update state when the user switches. When testing, simulate a user who connects on Mainnet while your app expects Sepolia: confirm your detection code prompts a clear instruction and prevents dangerous transactions. Closing question: after adding detection, how will your dApp present the risk when a chain mismatch occurs so the user can respond safely? Wallet connection and network detection means subscribe to chainchanged and accountschanged, compare chainid to your target, and prompt safe network switches.. In practical terms, detect chainid, handle events, and guide the user to the correct network. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Always confirm chain and accounts
keyIdea.text: Subscribe to chainChanged and accountsChanged, compare chainId to your target, and prompt safe network switches.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.4 › Wallet Connection
Pattern

Detect and react to chain changes

Subscribe to window.ethereum events, get chainId via web3.eth.getChainId, and compare to your target chain.

Event handlers to implement
  • chainChanged: reload or update chain state and block risky actions
  • accountsChanged: update the active account and re-fetch balances
Concrete scenario
User connects on Mainnet while your dApp targets Sepolia. Your detection triggers a prompt and calls wallet_switchEthereumChain to request Sepolia.
Example Code (excerpt)
// Using Web3 and the injected provider
if (window.ethereum) {
  const web3 = new Web3(window.ethereum);
  // get numeric chain id
  web3.eth.getChainId().then(id => { console.log('Connected chainId:', id); });
  // listen for changes
  window.ethereum.on('chainChanged', (chainIdHex) => {
    // parse hex chain id and update state
    const dec = parseInt(chainIdHex, 16);
    console.log('chain changed to', dec);
    window.location.reload();
  });
  window.ethereum.on('accountsChanged', (accounts) => {
    console.log('accounts changed', accounts);
  });
}
Common mistake

Assuming the chain never changes during a session. Users can switch networks externally; your UI must adapt.

screens.title: Programmatic network switching
screens.subtitle: Requesting a wallet to switch chains and handling errors

narration.text: When your dApp detects a chain mismatch, you can ask the wallet to switch networks rather than forcing the user to open MetaMask manually. The key call is wallet_switchEthereumChain with the target chainId in hex. Implement this with error handling: if the wallet throws an error code 4902, the network is not added to the wallet and you should present instructions to add it; other errors should be surfaced with clear messaging so the user understands why switching failed. A concrete example is requesting Sepolia using chainId '0xaa36a7'; if the request succeeds, the wallet will prompt the user to confirm. A common misconception is that programmatic switching adds a network implicitly; it does not add unknown networks without additional metadata. Always prepare a graceful fallback path and clear UI guidance so users can add the network manually if needed. After implementing switch requests, test both success and the 4902 failure path to ensure the user experience remains clear. Programmatic network switching means request a chain switch with error handling and instruct users how to add missing networks when needed.. In practical terms, requesting a wallet to switch chains and handling errors. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Use wallet_switchEthereumChain carefully
keyIdea.text: Request a chain switch with error handling and instruct users how to add missing networks when needed.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.4 › Network Switching
Pattern

Request switch with fallback

Call wallet_switchEthereumChain and handle the 4902 error by showing add-network instructions.

User flow
  1. Detect wrong chain
  2. Request wallet_switchEthereumChain
  3. If code 4902: show add-network guidance
  4. If other error: show helpful message and logging
Example Code
const targetChainId = '0xaa36a7';

async function switchNetwork() {
  try {
    await window.ethereum.request({
      method: 'wallet_switchEthereumChain',
      params: [{ chainId: targetChainId }],
    });
  } catch (switchError) {
    if (switchError.code === 4902) {
      // Network not added to wallet. Provide instructions to user.
      console.error('Network not found. Please add it to your wallet.');
    } else {
      console.error('Failed to switch network:', switchError);
    }
  }
}
Gotcha

Do not assume switch requests always succeed. Provide a clear fallback and message for the user to add the network manually.

screens.title: Input validation and sanitization
screens.subtitle: Using web3.utils.isAddress, numeric checks, and BigNumber conversions

narration.text: Input validation in a dApp reduces accidental mistakes and stops many simple attacks. Define input validation as the process of checking user-provided values for expected format and range before using them in Web3 calls. For addresses, web3. utils. isAddress returns whether a string is a syntactically valid Ethereum address; it does not guarantee ownership or that the address corresponds to the intended recipient, so you should still surface the address and let the user confirm it. For amounts, check for positive numbers, reject NaN and negative values, and convert to Wei safely using web3. utils. toWei or a BigNumber library to avoid precision loss. A common misconception is that client-side validation is enough — always repeat critical checks on the backend or in contract logic where possible. Concrete example: a transfer form should reject an address that fails isAddress and show a red inline error, and it should convert a valid '0.1' ether input to Wei before building the transaction payload. Final reflective question: how will you present formatted values back to the user so they can confirm before signing?

keyIdea.title: Validate format and range
keyIdea.text: Use web3.utils.isAddress for addresses, numeric checks for amounts, and convert to Wei to avoid precision errors.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.4 › Input Validation
Checks

Address and amount validation

  • Use web3.utils.isAddress to reject malformed addresses.
  • Require numeric, positive amounts and convert to Wei with web3.utils.toWei.
  • Show formatted values back to the user for confirmation before signing.
Concrete example
If web3.utils.isAddress returns false, present an inline error and disable submit. For amount '0.5', convert to Wei to build the transaction value.
Example Form
Transfer form pseudo-UI
Recipient address input, amount input, inline errors, and a disabled transfer button until checks pass. Convert to Wei and display both human and machine values for confirmation.
// Validation steps
if (!web3.utils.isAddress(recipientAddress)) {
  setError('Invalid Ethereum address.');
  return;
}
const parsed = parseFloat(amount);
if (isNaN(parsed) || parsed <= 0) {
  setError('Amount must be a positive number.');
  return;
}
const amountInWei = web3.utils.toWei(amount, 'ether');
// proceed with transaction using amountInWei
Key Takeaway

Validate format and convert units before sending. Always present values back to the user for confirmation.

screens.title: Protecting users from phishing and malicious interactions
screens.subtitle: Design UI flows to reveal transaction details and reject dangerous prompts

narration.text: Phishing in a Web3 context often looks like a prompt that asks users to sign messages or transactions without making consequences clear. The defensive claim is simple: always show the to address, value, and any function data or message contents in human-readable terms before the user signs. For contracts, show the function name and the arguments rather than raw hex data when possible; for message signing, show the actual message text and explain its effect. A concrete example: when a dApp asks the user to sign a transaction that transfers tokens, display the destination address, token symbol, and amount in plain language and require an explicit confirmation. A common misconception is that users will inspect raw hex or copy-paste addresses — they usually will not. So use clear labels, warnings for uncommon actions, and confirmations for high-value transfers. Ending question: how will you surface unusual contract calls so users understand if a prompt is suspicious? Protecting users from phishing and malicious interactions means surface human-friendly transaction details and explain message signing to reduce phishing risks.. In practical terms, design ui flows to reveal transaction details and reject dangerous prompts. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Make signing understandable
keyIdea.text: Surface human-friendly transaction details and explain message signing to reduce phishing risks.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.4 › Phishing Protection
Principle

Show human-friendly transaction context

Translate function calls and data into readable descriptions and require explicit consent for unexpected actions.

Example
When requesting a transfer, show the recipient address, token symbol, and the amount in a short confirmation dialog before signing.
Common mistake

Showing only raw hex or a generic 'Sign' prompt. This leaves users unable to judge the action's effect.

UX checklist
  • Display to-address, value, and decoded function name and args
  • Label message-signing content clearly and explain consequences
  • Flag high-value or uncommon calls with an extra confirmation
Analogy
Treat signing like authorizing a bank transfer: show recipient and amount before asking for approval.

screens.title: API key management and backend proxying
screens.subtitle: Why keys must stay on a server and how to proxy provider requests

narration.text: A P I keys for node providers and pinning services belong on a backend, not in the browser. Frontend code is public, so embedding keys allows attackers to extract them and abuse your provider quota or cause costs. The recommended architecture is a simple proxy: the frontend makes authenticated requests to your backend, which holds the A P I key in an environment variable and forwards the request to Infura, Alchemy, or Pinata. This preserves the key, allows rate limiting, logging, and quota control, and lets you add server-side validation before forwarding calls. A concrete example: instead of initializing Web3 with an Infura URL embedded in the React bundle, have your React app call /api/blockchain/read on your server, and have the server perform the Infura request using the stored project ID. A common misconception is that obfuscation prevents key theft; it does not. Takeaway: move secrets server-side, apply rate limiting, and log requests so abuse can be detected early. API key management and backend proxying means proxy provider calls through a backend that stores api keys as environment variables and enforces rate limits.. In practical terms, why keys must stay on a server and how to proxy provider requests. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Keep keys server-side
keyIdea.text: Proxy provider calls through a backend that stores API keys as environment variables and enforces rate limits.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.4 › API Key Management
Architecture

Frontend → Backend → Provider

Move all provider API keys to a backend process and let the backend make authenticated calls.

Benefits
  • Hide keys from users and crawlers
  • Apply rate limiting and logging
  • Validate requests server-side before forwarding
Proxy example
Frontend calls your /api/blockchain endpoint. Backend reads API key from environment and calls provider. Return only necessary data to the frontend.
Deployment note
Store API keys in environment variables, never check them into version control, and rotate keys if suspect abuse is detected.
Misconception

Putting keys in client code is safe if you obfuscate. In reality obfuscation is reversible and keys will leak.

screens.title: Dependency security and rate limiting
screens.subtitle: Audit packages and throttle backend endpoints

narration.text: Third-party packages and open-source dependencies power dApp frontends, but they can introduce vulnerabilities. Define two practical actions: audit dependencies regularly and implement server-side rate limiting. Use npm or yarn audit to find known issues in package. json, and apply updates or mitigations before production deployment. For your backend proxy endpoints, implement rate limiting so a leaked A P I key or a malicious client cannot exhaust your provider quotas. A concrete scenario: an attacker obtains a leaked key and fires repeated requests to your proxy; with rate limiting, you can cap requests per IP or user and log suspicious activity to block and rotate keys. A common misconception is that only large projects get attacked; in fact, exposed keys and unbounded endpoints are attractive targets at any scale. Takeaway: combine dependency audits and rate-limited proxies to make abuse expensive and detectable. Dependency security and rate limiting means keep dependencies updated with audits and protect provider usage with rate limiting and logging on backend endpoints.. In practical terms, audit packages and throttle backend endpoints. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Audit and throttle
keyIdea.text: Keep dependencies updated with audits and protect provider usage with rate limiting and logging on backend endpoints.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.4 › Dependencies & Rate Limiting
Dependency hygiene

Audit and update

Run package audits, review reported vulnerabilities, and apply updates or pin safe versions before release.

Quick checklist
  • Run npm audit or yarn audit periodically
  • Review transitive dependencies for wallet-related packages
  • Test after upgrades to confirm behavior
Rate limiting

Protect provider usage

Limit calls per IP or per user token, and log anomalies so you can rotate keys when abuse is detected.

Example
Add a simple bucket limiter on your /api/blockchain endpoint to cap requests over a short window and return a clear error when the limit is reached.

screens.title: Implement network switching and validation
screens.subtitle: A guided exercise to add checks to your React dApp

narration.text: This hands-on activity walks you through adding network switching and basic input validation to a React dApp. Start by wrapping your app with a NetworkChecker component that requests accounts and reads the chainId, subscribes to chainChanged and accountsChanged events, and conditionally blocks the main UI when the chain does not match your target. Next, create a TransferForm that validates recipient addresses with web3. utils. isAddress and validates numeric amounts to be positive. Convert valid amounts to Wei using web3. utils. toWei before sending the transaction. Replace any hard-coded provider keys by moving calls to a server endpoint that holds keys in environment variables. Test by connecting MetaMask to a wrong chain and observing the prompt to switch, then attempt a transfer with an invalid address to see the inline error. A common pitfall is not testing the 4902 error path when switching networks — include it in your flow. Final check: can you reproduce each milestone described earlier? If yes, you have implemented the core protections covered in this chapter. Implement network switching and validation means implement networkchecker and transferform, test wrong-network flows and input errors, and move keys to a backend proxy.. In practical terms, a guided exercise to add checks to your react dapp. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Practice makes secure
keyIdea.text: Implement NetworkChecker and TransferForm, test wrong-network flows and input errors, and move keys to a backend proxy.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.4 › Activity
Steps
  1. Wrap App with NetworkChecker: request accounts and getChainId, handle chainChanged and accountsChanged.
  2. Add switchNetwork using wallet_switchEthereumChain with proper 4902 handling.
  3. Create TransferForm: validate web3.utils.isAddress and numeric positivity, convert to Wei.
  4. Move any Infura or provider keys to a backend proxy and test the frontend calls the proxy.
  5. Simulate wrong-network and invalid-input flows and confirm UI blocks or shows errors.
Hints
  • Use parseInt(chainIdHex, 16) to convert hex chain IDs to decimal for comparisons.
  • Disable submit buttons while validation fails and show inline error messages.
  • On the backend, require an API key or token for your proxy to limit abuse.
Key Takeaway

Build, test, and verify each defensive control. Reproduce failure modes so your UX handles them gracefully.

screens.title: Assessment: network mismatch and API key risks
screens.subtitle: Two practical questions to test your understanding

narration.text: This assessment gives two scenario-based questions that mirror real decisions you'll make in a dApp. First scenario: a user is connected to Mainnet while your dApp is intended for Sepolia. Explain the potential user and dApp problems, such as failed transactions or accidental real ETH transfers if a different contract exists on Mainnet, and list the programmatic steps your app should take: detect chainId, compare to target, prompt the user, and request wallet_switchEthereumChain with a clear fallback for 4902. Second scenario: an Infura project ID is placed directly in React code. Explain why this is risky — keys are publicly visible, can be abused to exhaust quotas or incur cost, and may enable denial-of-service against your app — and describe the recommended solution of moving keys to a backend proxy stored as environment variables with rate limiting. These scenarios map directly to the work you implemented in the hands-on activity and give clear criteria for grading practical security controls. Assessment: network mismatch and API key risks means use scenario-based assessments: chain mismatch handling and moving keys off the frontend are measurable proof of competency.. In practical terms, two practical questions to test your understanding. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. narration.text: These three core concepts capture the highest-value ideas from the chapter. First, wallet connection security: always ensure users are connected to the intended network and provide a safe path to switch to it. Second, window. ethereum is the injected provider object that exposes chain and account information and event hooks; use it to listen for changes and to request network switches. Third, input validation means verifying addresses and numeric values before building transactions so your app never sends malformed data. Each of these concepts leads to direct actions you can take in code: read chainId, subscribe to events, call web3. utils. isAddress, and convert amounts to Wei. Remember these three as the minimal, actionable checklist you should apply to every dApp screen that initiates blockchain interactions. Key Concepts — Part 1 means ensure correct network, use the injected provider safely, and validate all user inputs before signing.. In practical terms, core terms and quick reminders. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: High-value reminders
keyIdea.text: Ensure correct network, use the injected provider safely, and validate all user inputs before signing.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.4 › Key Concepts
Wallet Connection Security
Ensure users are on the target network and handle chain/account changes gracefully.
window.ethereum
The injected provider object that exposes chainId, accounts, and event hooks to your dApp.
Input Validation
Check address format and numeric ranges, and convert units before building transactions.
Summary

These three practices are quick wins: confirm network, use the injected provider safely, and validate inputs before signing.

narration.text: These final three concepts focus on operational controls you should build into your dApp. First, phishing attacks: never ask for private keys or mnemonics, and always present clear signing information so users can spot suspicious requests. Second, A P I key management: never embed provider keys in the frontend; instead, use a backend proxy that stores keys in environment variables and enforces rate limits and logging. Third, rate limiting: apply quotas to backend endpoints to prevent abuse and preserve provider capacity. Each of these reduces real-world risks: phishing protections reduce human error, backend proxies prevent key theft, and rate limits make attacks expensive. Final reflection: which of these controls would you implement immediately and which would you schedule into your next release? Key Concepts — Part 2 means protect users from phishing, keep keys server-side, and apply rate limiting to make abuse difficult.. In practical terms, operational controls and protective patterns. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Operational security
keyIdea.text: Protect users from phishing, keep keys server-side, and apply rate limiting to make abuse difficult.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.4 › Operational Controls
Phishing Attacks
Never request private keys; always show clear transaction summaries to reduce deception risk.
API Key Management
Store keys in environment variables on a backend proxy and never in client bundles.
Rate Limiting
Throttle backend endpoints to limit abuse and preserve provider quotas.
Final takeaway
